blocks.en: Hello, young explorers, and welcome back to Michael's Morning Listening!
Today we meet heroes with four legs and wet noses.
First, five rescue dogs who have retired — and found new families.
Then, the secret inside a dog's nose: why can it smell things we cannot even imagine?
Ready?
Let's go!
In Ecuador, five rescue dogs have just retired.
Their names are Ares, Kratos, Zeus, Titan and Gaia.
For seven years, they worked with firefighters, looking for people after earthquakes and landslides.
They were German shepherds and golden retrievers, and their approach was simple: follow the nose, never give up.
It was not easy.
They climbed over broken stones and searched through dust, rain and heat.
More than once, a dog found a person under the stones — and the rescuers could feel the person's pulse.
He was alive!
The dogs did not just save lives; they gave families hope again.
Now the five heroes are off duty.
At a ceremony, the firefighters said thank you, and each dog went home with a new family.
Gaia's new owner, Valeria, said she could not believe her new pet used to save lives.
Now Gaia's job is easier: long walks, good food, and a soft bed.
After years of hard work, these heroes have earned their rest.
So how does a dog's nose do such amazing work?
Here is one amazing aspect: a dog's sense of smell is 10,000 to 100,000 times more sensitive than ours.
Inside a dog's nose there are up to 300 million smell receptors — tiny scent sensors.
We humans have only about six million.
And the part of a dog's brain that reads smells is about 40 times bigger than ours.
How does it work?
When a dog sniffs, air goes into two rooms inside its nose: one for breathing, one for smelling.
The smelling room is full of soft tissue that traps scent, so the smell stays after the dog breathes out.
That is why a dog can follow a trail hours later — and tell which way a person walked, sniffing left, then right.
Scientists conducted an experiment: they trained dogs to smell sickness in people's breath — and the dogs could do it!
Dogs can smell things at one part in a trillion.
Imagine one drop in twenty swimming pools — that is how tiny a smell a dog can catch.
When your dog wrinkles its forehead and sniffs the air, it is reading a whole world you cannot see.
Today's idiom is "off the hook." It means you are free from a job or a trouble — you do not have to do it anymore.
For example: Gaia worked for seven years, and now she is off the hook — no more rescues, naps and games!
In your life: you thought you had to clean your room, but Mum says, "You are off the hook today!" Try it this week: tell your family about a time you were off the hook!
Now it is your turn!
Two questions for you.
One: Gaia's new life is long walks and soft beds.
If you adopted a hero dog, what would you do on its first day at home?
Two: a dog can smell one drop in twenty swimming pools.
What smell would you most like to have a dog's nose for?
Talk about it with your family!
That is all for today, young explorers.
We appreciate you listening and learning with us.
Keep your eyes open, keep asking questions, and we will meet tomorrow morning.
Goodbye, and have a wonderful day!
